hook_text: Two classes, same test. Class B's average is higher. So B did better, right? The numbers say something more interesting.
clip_script: Two classes of ten wrote the same test out of 50. Class A averaged 38.0. Class B averaged 38.6. So B did better? Slow down. Line up Class A: 23, 31, 35, 35, 38, 40, 42, 44, 45, 47. Line up Class B: 30, 33, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41, 43, 49. The middles are nearly the same: medians of 39 and 38.5. The spreads are not. A runs from 23 to 47, a range of 24. B runs from 30 to 49, a range of 19. B is the steadier class. A has a straggler at 23 and B has the top mark of 49. So the honest comparison is: about the same in the middle, B more consistent, A with one low mark. And with ten learners each, a gap of 0.6 in the mean proves nothing about the teaching. Never compare two sets with one number. Middle AND spread, both with values. Say it: same middle, different spread.
visual_style: Two rows of ten dots on a shared number line from 20 to 50, Class A above and Class B below; the medians light up almost aligned; the ranges stretch as coloured bars of different lengths; the lone 23 glows as a straggler.
pacing: The tempting conclusion fast, the two line-ups at speaking pace, the spread reveal with a beat, the honest conclusion slow.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for reading graphs critically, two rainfall lines that cross, and comparing schools of different sizes.
